hook: The physiological signs of anxiety and excitement are almost identical. The difference happens in the first two seconds — and you can influence it.
topic: Anxiety vs. excitement — cognitive labelling and the two-second window
body:
**The physiological signs of anxiety and excitement are almost identical.**

Elevated heart rate. Faster breathing. Heightened alertness. Narrowed focus. Butterflies.

These are not uniquely anxiety symptoms. They are your threat-and-opportunity-response system activating — the same underlying arousal state, regardless of what triggered it.

The difference between anxiety and excitement in these moments is almost entirely in the story your brain tells about the signal in the first two seconds. If the narrative is "this is dangerous," the experience becomes anxiety. If the narrative is "this is important," the same activation can be channelled as preparation.

This isn't wishful thinking. Research on what's called cognitive reappraisal shows that labelling activation as excitement rather than anxiety — even without fully believing it — measurably changes both physiological response and performance outcomes.

The window is narrow. Once the anxiety narrative is established, changing it becomes much harder. But in the first two seconds of noticing the signal — before the spiral starts — there is a genuine point of influence.

Notice the activation. Name it differently. "My body is preparing." That's not denial. That's accurate — and it uses the same arousal state as a resource.

The full technique is in the free guide in my bio.
